claims.text: Lowering the ethanol-oxidation temperature from 60°C to 25°C decreases in situ formation of surface hydroxyl species on nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Surface hydroxyl coverage modulates the adsorption–desorption balance of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Hydroxyl-mediated changes in intermediate adsorption and desorption shift catalytic activity.
Hydroxyl-mediated changes in intermediate adsorption and desorption shift ethanol-oxidation product selectivity.
The freshly synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts have a uniform elemental distribution.
The freshly synthesized PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts have a uniform surface structure.
The controlled intervention is a temperature decrease from a 60°C baseline to 25°C.
Adsorbed hydroxyl species can form on the surface of the catalyst.
Surface hydroxyl formation and coverage are temperature-dependent over 25–60°C.
Adsorbed hydroxyl species alter the electronic environment of active sites.
Adsorbed hydroxyl species alter the steric environment of active sites.
At lower temperature, the rate of hydroxyl formation is reduced, producing lower adsorbed-hydroxyl coverage.
Lower hydroxyl coverage can promote different ethanol-oxidation pathways.
At 25°C, hydroxyl-related in situ infrared peak intensity will be lower than at 60°C.
At 25°C, catalytic current densities will differ from those measured at 60°C and will correlate with lower hydroxyl coverage.
At 25°C, the product distribution will shift relative to 60°C and may show increased acetaldehyde formation.
The proposed mechanism applies only where temperature significantly modulates hydroxyl kinetics without introducing additional mass-transport effects.
The proposed mechanism applies only where temperature does not introduce additional reaction-pathway changes.
A performance change without a corresponding hydroxyl-coverage change, or failure of artificial hydroxyl modification at 60°C to affect performance, would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that lower hydroxyl coverage may promote different reaction pathways, while the stated boundary requires a temperature range in which no additional reaction-pathway changes occur.
